subtitle: 34 · referred by her GP after her brother died suddenly
opening: Hello. My GP said you would want to ask me about my family.

questions.q: What has brought you to the clinic today?
questions.a: My little brother Kofi died last year. He collapsed while he was playing football. The post-mortem said he had a heart condition – hypertrophic cardiomyopathy – and the heart team found a change in one of his genes. They said the rest of the family should be seen. I'm pregnant, so I'm worried about my children as well.

questions.q: How old are you, Abena?
Have you had any heart symptoms yourself, such as palpitations, blackouts or chest pain?
questions.a: No blackouts and no chest pain. I get out of breath on the stairs, but I'm pregnant, so I don't know what's normal. The cardiologist has booked me a heart scan.

questions.q: And apart from Kofi, everyone in the family is healthy, I assume?
questions.a: Um… I think so. I haven't really thought about it.
questions.poor: A leading question suggests the answer you expect, and it can hide exactly what you need to know. Ask about each relative in turn instead, for example: ‘How is your father's health?’

questions.q: Do you have a partner?
questions.a: Yes, my husband James. He's 36.

questions.q: Are you and James related to each other in any way, for example as cousins?
questions.a: No. James's family are from the Volta Region and mine are from around Kumasi. We met at university.
questions.note: Ask every couple about consanguinity. A plain question such as this one is easier to answer than a technical word.

questions.q: Do you have any children?
questions.a: Two. Ella is six and Noah is three. And I'm twelve weeks pregnant.

questions.q: Have you had any other pregnancies?
questions.a: I had a miscarriage at about ten weeks, in 2021. That was between Ella and Noah.
questions.note: Draw pregnancy losses in birth order with the other children: a small triangle between Ella and Noah.

questions.q: How are Ella and Noah?
questions.a: They're both well. Nobody has checked their hearts yet – that's one of the things I want to ask about.

questions.q: Do you have any brothers or sisters?
questions.a: Two brothers. I'm the eldest, then Kwesi, who's 31. Kofi was the youngest.

questions.q: Do you all have the same mother and father?
questions.a: Yes, we do.

questions.q: When did Kofi pass?
questions.a: Pass…? Oh – you mean when did he die. Last March. He was 28.
questions.poor: Euphemisms such as ‘pass’ can be unclear, and some people find them awkward. Plain words are kinder in the end: ‘How old was Kofi when he died?’

questions.q: How old was Kofi when he died, and what happened?
questions.a: He was 28. He collapsed playing five-a-side football last March, and they couldn't bring him round. The post-mortem found a thickened heart muscle – hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

questions.q: Great, thank you. And what about your parents?
questions.a: (She pauses.) …Right. Yes. My parents.
questions.poor: Fillers such as ‘great’ can sound careless straight after someone has described a death. Acknowledge it first: ‘I'm sorry. That must have been a terrible shock for your family.’

questions.q: I'm sorry about Kofi. That must have been a terrible shock for all of you.
questions.a: Thank you. It still doesn't feel real. Mum finds it very hard to talk about.
questions.note: Acknowledging a loss before you move on is part of taking a family history well. Sharing your sense of what the person may be feeling is called ‘tentative immediacy’ (see the top tips above).

questions.q: Did Kofi have a partner or any children?
questions.a: He had a girlfriend, but they didn't have any children.

questions.q: How is Kwesi's health, and does he have any children?
questions.a: He's well. He had a heart scan in the summer and they said it was normal. He isn't married and he hasn't got children.

questions.q: Are both of your parents still living?
questions.a: Yes. Dad is 63 and Mum is 61.

questions.q: How is your father's health?
questions.a: He has high blood pressure. After Kofi died, the heart team scanned all of us. They said Dad has a thickened heart muscle too – the same condition as Kofi – but he feels fine.

questions.q: How is your mother's health?
questions.a: She's well. Her heart scan was normal.

questions.q: Are your parents related to each other?
questions.a: No, not as far as I know.

questions.q: Does your father have any brothers or sisters?
questions.a: Yes. He's the youngest of three. Auntie Adwoa is 68 and Uncle Kojo is 66.

questions.q: How is your Auntie Adwoa's health?
questions.a: She had a pacemaker fitted a few years ago. I don't know why – it isn't something the family talks about.

questions.q: Is that something you could ask your father or your aunt about?
questions.a: I could ask Dad. She's quite a private person, though.
questions.note: Write down what you don't know as well as what you do (‘pacemaker, reason not known’), and whether the patient can find out. A pacemaker could be relevant in a family with a heart condition.

questions.q: How is your Uncle Kojo?
questions.a: He's fine, as far as I know.

questions.q: Are your father's parents still living?
questions.a: Grandma Efua is 88 and still lives in Kumasi. Grandad Yaw died when Dad was a teenager.

questions.q: How old was your grandfather Yaw when he died, and do you know why he died?
questions.a: He was 45. He died in his sleep. The family always said it was his heart, but nobody really knows.
questions.note: A sudden death at 45 is important in this family. Record it as reported (‘d. 45, died suddenly in his sleep’) rather than shading him as affected, because the cause was never confirmed.

questions.q: Does your mother have any brothers or sisters?
questions.a: Three younger brothers. They're all in their fifties and all well.

questions.q: Have any of them had heart problems?
questions.a: Not that I know of. They've all been told about Kofi.
questions.note: When several relatives have nothing relevant to record, one symbol with the number inside (a square with 3 in it) keeps the pedigree tidy.

questions.q: Are your mother's parents still living?
questions.a: No. Grandad Kwasi died at 81 after a stroke, and Grandma Ama died at 79. She had diabetes.

questions.q: Originally, where did each of your grandparents come from?
questions.a: All four were from Ghana, from around Kumasi.

questions.q: Has anyone in the family been seen by a genetics service or had a genetic test?
questions.a: Only Kofi. They tested a sample from his post-mortem and found a change in a gene called MYBPC3. Dad, Mum and Kwesi are waiting to be tested.

questions.q: Has anyone else in the family died suddenly or at a young age?
questions.a: Just Grandad Yaw, and Kofi.

questions.q: Has anyone fainted or had a fit during exercise?
questions.a: Not that I know of.

questions.q: Is there anything else you think I should know, or anything you want to ask?
questions.a: Only that I'm worried about Ella and Noah, and the baby. Will they need tests?
questions.note: Before you finish, check that you have what you need, date and sign the pedigree, and tell the patient how to contact you if they remember something later.
